strongest_objection: A 16.4‑hour continuous overflow recorded by an online EDM monitor, with virtually zero rainfall at two gauges – the nearest only 0.8 km away – is inconsistent with a brief sensor glitch or missed rain, making a genuine dry‑spill the most plausible explanation.

case.summary: Storm overflow NWL00415 (Northumbrian Water) discharging into Dawdon Dene Beck began a spill at 2026-11-14 18:26:20 UTC. The spill has no recorded end time and has lasted 16.4 hours, with the monitor reported online (monitor_offline: false). Rainfall at both nearby Environment Agency gauges was negligible. Station 025878, 0.8 km away, recorded 0.2 mm in the 24h before, 0.0 mm in the 24–48h before, and 0.0 mm during the spill. Station 026090, 7.5 km away, recorded 0.0 mm in all three windows. The maxima across gauges were 0.2 mm (0–24h before), 0.0 mm (24–48h before) and 0.0 mm (during). The feed classifies the event as a 'dry_spill_candidate'. With essentially no rain before or during a 16.4-hour discharge, there is no apparent heavy-rain justification, so this is a potential permit breach. There are no prior cases at this site in memory. The company's record in memory is 1 case, 1 likely breach, across 1 site.
breach_indicators: Zero rainfall (0.0 mm) recorded during the spill at both gauges (025878 at 0.8 km, 026090 at 7.5 km).
Only 0.2 mm of rain in the 24 hours before the spill, at the closest gauge (0.8 km); 0.0 mm at the 7.5 km gauge.
0.0 mm of rain in the 24–48 hours before the spill at both gauges, so no recent wet antecedent conditions are evident.
Spill duration of 16.4 hours with no recorded end (latesteventend: null), so the spill appears to be ongoing or unclosed.
Monitor reported online (monitor_offline: false), so the discharge signal is not obviously a monitor fault.
The closest rain gauge is only 0.8 km from the outfall, which strengthens the representativeness of the dry readings.
The company has 1 prior likely breach in memory (1 case, 1 site), though not at this site.

What is the Environmental Permit for NWL00415 and its consent conditions (e.g., pass-forward flow, storm tank requirements)?
Did the Environment Agency radar or other rain gauges near Dawdon/Seaham show any rainfall on 13–15 November 2026 that the two gauges missed?
Was there snowmelt, high groundwater or tidal influence around Dawdon Dene in mid-November 2026 that could cause infiltration-driven flows?
Did Northumbrian Water report any pumping station failure, blockage, power outage or asset fault at or upstream of this overflow around 14 November 2026?
Is the EDM monitor at NWL00415 known to give false positives? Has the company flagged the event as a monitor error?
Were there any Environment Agency pollution incident reports or public complaints for Dawdon Dene Beck or the adjacent coast around 14–15 November 2026?
What was the earlier likely-breach case for Northumbrian Water in our records, and does it show a similar pattern (e.g., the same catchment or the same failure mode)?

evidence.report:
I found nothing published that explains this spill innocently: no reported asset failure, no unexpected rain and no monitor-fault notice. One published source confirms the spill and gives an end time. A weather forecast supports the dry readings from the rain gauges. Most of the investigator's questions couldn't be answered from public sources. I used all 5 searches and 2 of 3 page reads.

## What the sources show

**1. The spill happened, and has since ended.**
- NWL00415 appears to be Northumbrian Water's **Dalton‑Le‑Dale CSO**, a storm overflow into Dawdon Dene Beck, in the Seaham Peterlee Coast catchment. https://www.floodmapper.co.uk/stations/dalton-le-dale-cso-dalton-le-dale/metric/bf40ffca-5ce5-408d-8641-649320a6455a
  - I matched it by name and river, not by the ID or coordinates, so the match should be confirmed.
- On the same page, the discharge **started 14 Nov 2026 at 6:26:20 PM**, the same time as our feed. It **ended 15 Nov 2026 at 11:01:21 AM**, about 995 minutes or 16.6 hours. It is the only event in the window shown.
  - That fills in our feed's missing end time and roughly matches its 16.4 hours.
- **Caveat:** FloodMapper is an independent site. It republishes data that the Environment Agency oversees and says it doesn't check that data. It is a reasonable copy of the company's monitor feed, but not an official record.

**2. The weather was dry.**
- The Northern Echo said Friday 13 Nov was chilly and sunny across County Durham, with frost forming overnight. It expected Saturday 14 Nov to stay "largely dry", with rain possible later only in north‑western areas. It said rain would arrive across parts of County Durham on Sunday 15 Nov. https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/
  - The page is labelled as written by sister title USA Today.
  - It is a **forecast published on 13 Nov, not measured rainfall**.
  - It doesn't say what time rain reached the Seaham coast on the 15th.

**3. No reported incident.**
- A search for blockages, pumping station failures or power cuts at Seaham, Dalton‑le‑Dale or Murton (7–25 Nov 2026) found **nothing**.
- A search for news of a sewage spill at Dawdon or Seaham in November 2026 also found **nothing**. Those results were about Dawdon's mine‑water scheme and bonus‑ban stories, which have nothing to do with this site.

## Findings

**Supports a breach**
- Published monitor data confirms a single continuous discharge of about 16.6 hours. It started at the time our feed gives, and there is no sign of a short sensor blip.
- The local paper expected 13–14 Nov to be dry and frosty across County Durham. Rain was only expected on the 15th, when the spill was already about 16 hours old. This matches the near‑zero readings at both gauges.
- I found no published pump failure, blockage or power cut that would explain an emergency discharge.

**Supports an innocent explanation**
- Nothing I found directly supports one.
- The Northern Echo forecast rain for parts of County Durham on 15 Nov. That could matter only for the last few hours before the 11:01 end, and both gauges recorded 0.0 mm during the spill.
- Missing news coverage doesn't prove there was no asset fault. Companies often don't publicise them.

**Unknown**
- The environmental permit and its conditions (pass‑forward flow, storm tank).
- The site's yearly spill counts and hours.
- Whether Northumbrian Water has flagged this event as a monitor error or an operational problem.
- Environment Agency incident reports or public complaints about this beck or coast.
- Tide, surge or groundwater effects. The outfall is near the coast, so this is still worth checking with the Environment Agency, but I found no evidence either way.
- Measured rainfall from radar or other gauges, as opposed to a forecast.
- Details of the company's earlier likely‑breach case.

**Overall:** the published evidence agrees with the dry‑spill flag and with the skeptic's 0.78 confidence. The most useful next step is to ask Northumbrian Water and the Environment Agency directly for the permit, any record of an asset fault or monitor error on 14–15 Nov, and tide and groundwater data.

objections_refuted: EDM sensor fault or spurious short blip: an independent republication of the monitor feed (FloodMapper) shows a single continuous discharge starting 14 Nov 18:26:20 and ending 15 Nov 11:01:21, about 16.6 hours.
Data-feed or timestamp error creating a phantom start: the same start time appears in an independent source.
Localized rain missed by the gauges: a contemporaneous forecast described 13–14 Nov as dry and frosty across County Durham, with rain only from 15 Nov. This matches 0.0–0.2 mm at a gauge 0.8 km away.
Snowmelt: there is no evidence of snow. The weather was frosty and sunny, and the skeptic itself rated this as low plausibility.
objections_standing: Emergency discharge from pump failure, blockage or power loss: no public report was found, but companies often don't publicise faults. Even if true, this would still be a reportable dry-day discharge.
Tidal backflow or surge at a near-coastal outfall: not checked, with no evidence either way.
High groundwater or infiltration: not verified. It is speculative given the dry antecedent conditions, so it carries limited weight.
Site identity match by name only: NWL00415 was matched to Dalton-le-Dale CSO by name and watercourse, not by ID or coordinates.
ruling.reasoning: Rainfall at both gauges was essentially zero across all windows, and the nearest gauge is only 0.8 km from the outfall. An independent copy of the monitor data confirms a continuous discharge of about 16.6 hours starting at the reported time. This rules out a sensor blip or a timestamp artefact. A local forecast corroborates dry weather on 13–14 Nov, with rain only on the 15th, when the spill was already well under way, and the gauges still show 0.0 mm during the spill. The remaining innocent explanations (asset failure, tidal influence, groundwater) are unverified and largely speculative. An asset failure would still warrant investigation as an unpermitted dry discharge. Residual uncertainty comes from the unofficial data source, the name-based site match, and the unchecked tidal and groundwater effects. A confidence slightly above the skeptic's 0.78 is warranted.

report:
# Evidence pack: possible dry-day discharge at NWL00415 (Northumbrian Water, Dawdon Dene Beck)

**Pipeline verdict:** likely_breach. **Adjudicated confidence:** 0.80.

## Summary

Storm overflow **NWL00415** (Northumbrian Water) discharges to **Dawdon Dene Beck** at 54.82785, -1.35538. It began spilling at **18:26:20 UTC on 14 Nov 2026**. The monitor was online.

- The feed showed the spill still open at 16.4 hours.
- An independent republication of the monitor data gives an end time of **11:01:21 on 15 Nov 2026**, a total of about **16.6 hours**.
- Rainfall at two nearby Environment Agency gauges was essentially zero before and during the spill. The nearer gauge is 0.8 km from the outfall.
- No published asset failure, monitor-fault notice or unexpected rainfall was found.

The pattern is consistent with a discharge in dry weather. Tidal, groundwater and asset-failure explanations have not been ruled out.

## The spill (data)

| Field | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Site ID | NWL00415 | Spill feed |
| Operator | Northumbrian Water | Spill feed |
| Receiving water | Dawdon Dene Beck | Spill feed |
| Location | 54.82785, -1.35538 | Spill feed |

| Duration | 16.4 h in feed (event still open); about 995 min (16.6 h) on FloodMapper | Both |
| Monitor offline | false | Spill feed |
| Automated flag | dry_spill_candidate | Spill feed |

**Site identity:** FloodMapper lists a Northumbrian Water monitor called **Dalton-Le-Dale CSO** discharging to Dawdon Dene Beck. The evidence agent matched it to NWL00415 **by name and watercourse only**, not by ID or coordinates. This match needs confirming.

**Data status:** FloodMapper is an independent site. It republishes data overseen by the Environment Agency and states that it does not verify that data. It is not an official record.

## Rainfall context

Environment Agency rain gauges (spill feed):

| Station | Distance | 0–24 h before | 24–48 h before | During spill |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 025878 | 0.8 km | 0.2 mm | 0.0 mm | 0.0 mm |
| 026090 | 7.5 km | 0.0 mm | 0.0 mm | 0.0 mm |
| **Max** | | **0.2 mm** | **0.0 mm** | **0.0 mm** |

**Supporting forecast:** The Northern Echo published a forecast on 13 Nov ([source](https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/)). It described:
- 13 Nov as chilly and sunny across County Durham, with frost overnight
- 14 Nov as expected to be "largely dry", with rain possible later only in north-western areas

**Caveats on the rainfall evidence:**
- The Northern Echo article is a forecast, not measured rainfall.
- The page is labelled as written by a sister title.
- It does not say when rain reached the Seaham coast on 15 Nov.
- The feed's "during" window appears to reflect a snapshot taken at 16.4 h. The last roughly 10 minutes before the 11:01 end may not be covered by the gauge figures.

## Innocent explanations considered

The skeptic's assessment, with the adjudicator's ruling:

| Explanation | Skeptic plausibility | Status |
|---|---|---|
| EDM sensor fault or short blip | Low | **Refuted.** FloodMapper shows a single continuous event of about 16.6 h. |
| Data-feed or timestamp error | Low | **Refuted.** The same start time appears in an independent source. |
| Localised rain missed by gauges | Low | **Largely refuted.** The gauge is 0.8 km away and the forecast was dry for 13–14 Nov. |
| Snowmelt | Low | **Refuted.** No evidence of snow before the event. |
| High groundwater or infiltration | Medium | **Standing, unverified.** Limited weight given the dry antecedent conditions. |
| Tidal backflow or surge (outfall near the coast) | Medium | **Standing, unverified.** No evidence either way. |
| Emergency discharge from pump failure, blockage or power loss | Medium | **Standing.** No public report found, but companies often do not publicise faults. A discharge like this would still be a dry-day discharge warranting investigation. |
